records.statement: A readability score is not a text's difficulty: judge difficulty from the exact excerpt students read, by reading it as well as by formula.

records.statement: An item, its options, hints and pointers may require only what the student has met by then on every path, common knowledge, or what the item or reference materials supply.
records.detail: The reading project's lint checks that what a lesson assumes is a subset of what earlier lessons in the unit added, in unit order. A weekly quality check still found a taught word that never appears in its lesson's passage, while three of that lesson's checks assessed the child on it. What the item supplies includes the student's reference materials, and a further value or principle must be given too. The same bound covers response forms: no item may require or grade a response form the lesson hasn't taught and modelled.
records.against: The lint has no baseline across units, so a unit's first lesson must assume nothing, and the spec says nothing about what a unit may assume on entry. What counts as standard course content was judged by a model, not checked against the course framework. The same contract loosens the rule for short-answer items, which may draw on the target fact plus reasonable outside knowledge (`APinceptbench/docs/GENERATOR_API_SPEC.md`), and the essay rubric gives a point for specific evidence beyond the documents (`APinceptbench/ap_benchmark/prompts/official_ap_prompts.py`). Read together, the bound is what the course taught, not a single fact or a single set of documents. It holds where the assessment supplies reference materials or a passage; where recall is the skill being tested, a recalled fact is the point. The check deliberately leaves out taught vocabulary and invented practice scenarios, which would otherwise be flagged falsely (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0234-misc-artifacts-gate-eval-checks-recovery.qmd`).

records.statement: Give a judge exactly what the student sees, one bounded question at a time.
records.detail:
Every failure the reading engine has had was a judge asked to rule with the evidence missing
(`grade3-reading/engine/skills/jev-verify/SKILL.md`). One of its checks was handed a bare question with no passage and

records.statement: No surface feature may single out the key: keep options alike in length, grammar, register and scope.
records.detail: Generated multiple-choice items were given to a model from another family with the passage withheld; it recovered the key for 62.7% of them, and the leaked items showed wrong options with absolute words, a key that was systematically the longest, wrong options that contradict each other, and keys that were the obvious balanced or textbook-sounding answer. Selection-from-the-text items leaked when the question or span wording signposted the right phrases, and in one unit they survived only with at least two competing spans of the same shape and a question the solver could not resolve without the text. Sorting items leaked when passage titles were the category labels, while neutral labels (Source A, Source B, Both) gave the construction that produced 700 certified items, and two-part answer-and-evidence items with elaborate options were left out because one part could solve the other. The key is never the longest, shortest, most specific, most hedged, odd one out or only option sharing a distinctive word with the stem or source. Use no absolute words or 'all/none of the above'. Check lengths in code, item by item and across the set, and move reasoning from the key into its feedback where it runs long.
records.against: A length cue matters only where length can be exploited: a review left a sorting item's uniquely short extra alone, because extras are not keyed to prompts (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW-2026-09-04-R16.md`, line 52). Removing cues does not fix leaks whose cause is the passage: for the same generator's items, the report judged the leak not fixable with option-length patches (`grade3-reading/artifacts/LANE2_GENERATOR.md`, line 31). a blind solver that guessed from option length and wording flagged items that needed the passage and were clean, so a solver's guess alone does not prove a cue. The measured effect comes from four exams at one institution and covers item-writing flaws of every kind; the AP rule is a stated criterion with no count of failures; and a research summary warns that the most plausible wrong options are also the likeliest to be learned as true when no feedback follows. The same generator's structure judge is told that "Sentence length alone (unless extreme like a phrase vs. paragraph)" is not a structural difference (`icloud-work/incept/sat-reading-generation/sat-prompts.json`, line 80), leaving length to the code check. A grades 9-10 reading generator makes the cue a fixed rule, "The correct answer MUST NEVER be the longest option." (`icloud-work/incept/incept-multilingual-generation/src/external_submodules/reading-question-qc/ck_gen - prompts.json`, line 12, and again on lines 6, 18, 48 and 54); a key that is never the longest is a pattern of its own. The absolute-language list also catches ordinary words such as only, so a word filter can fail sound options (`icloud-work/evaluator/ap_benchmark/hard_fail/rules.py`, line 38). And the pipeline's fixed key order, 'Use locked answer keys A, C, and B in that order.' (`icloud-work/evaluatorML/.agent/memory/e2e_pipeline/iterate_repair_to_100.py`, line 201), balances each set but repeats one position pattern across every set, which is itself a surface cue. A word ban is blunt: one validation rule fails a true statement for its absolute words (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/validation_rules.md`). The writer's banned-word list had no enforcement, absolute language still appeared in 35% of items, and no rate after enforcement is recorded (`icloud-work/k_12_social_studies/python/improvement_plan_prompts.md`). The length cue rests on guidance, not on a measured case. Ordinary topic-word overlap is acceptable (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/sat_rw_evaluation.txt`, lines 75-76), and a single echo of a category label is borderline unless it is the dominant word in the label (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/match_evaluation.txt`, line 379). records.statement: Each wrong option must attract a student who misunderstood, and only the tested knowledge or the text may rule it out, never common sense or surface cues.
records.detail: An AP evaluator's rubric fails a question when a wrong option can be ruled out by general reasoning, test-taking instinct or surface cues without the content the item assesses, which turns it into a logic puzzle; it names absolutes that carry the claim, self-contradiction with the stem, claims false on their face and options off the stem's named topic, and a guard catches the right answer being the only option that repeats a distinctive word from the stem. Before the fix, a question whose wrong options were all implausible or giveaways still passed at ~0.91, because one zeroed score was averaged away; after it, the reproducer went from PASS@0.9143 to failing ~80% of runs, with distractor_quality=0.0 in 23-25/30. No wrong option may be rejectable by common sense, a sweeping absolute, a contradiction of the stem or of another option, being true of any text on the topic, or lying outside the question's topic, period or category, and none may be generic filler. Each wrong option should also attract a student who misunderstood.
records.against: Keyed to surface words the rule over-fired: the model treated any absolute word as a giveaway and failed sound items, so it was narrowed to absolutes that carry the claim, and the rubric now warns that an option that is merely incorrect is not a giveaway. The code guard for negations fires only when every key follows the stem's direction and every wrong option opposes it (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/evaluators/guards.py`, lines 962-974). The shares are among leaked items only; no rate for clean items is given (`grade3-reading/artifacts/alpha-read-packager/generator/g5/GENERATOR_REPAIR_KIT.md`, lines 13-15). A review accepted obviously wrong options in an end-of-lesson fill-in: "For blank 3, `charged`/`marched` "into the night" are grammatical but clearly wrong, which is acceptable." (`shadow-content-eval/reports/G3-U1-L14-review.md`, line 100). The training report's claim that fill-in passes at twice the multiple-choice rate does not match its own table, which gives 30.7% against 23.2% and 17.9% (`icloud-work/incept/ML_TRAINING_INSIGHTS_REPORT.md`, lines 293-295 and 430). A first attempt at same-theme wrong options for one item regressed to 1 of 3 and was reverted, reason not given, and the report warns that such options must not become defensible alternate keys. The two misses were stopped by the solver's own scope check, not by a grader verdict: "causing local rejection and then live IB timeout" (icloud-work/aptraining/workspace/comms/from_den/2026-05-22T2050Z_DELIVERED_pipeline_solver_v7_supersedes_v6.md, line 51). A word-usage check may rightly test one register violation with every wrong option, and one review downgraded the same-misuse finding to minor for that reason (`grade3-reading/artifacts/peter-pan-standing-2026-09-11/readiness-l5-2026-09-17/sim-review/agent-B-D5-D6-D11-D13.md`, line 21).
